Lincoln
LING-kun
n. (the largest medieval English diocese, the see of Robert Grosseteste and the diocese in which Wycliffe and Oxford lay)
From Latin Lindum Colonia, the colony at Lindum, from a British name for the pool.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Lincoln held the largest diocese in medieval England, running from the Humber to the Thames and including Oxford, so that every question raised in the university was in the end a Lincoln matter. Its greatest bishop was Robert Grosseteste, from 1235 to 1253, a scholar of Greek and of optics, translator of Aristotle and of the Greek fathers, and a reformer of ferocious energy: he visited every parish in the diocese, deprived incompetent clergy, insisted that rectors reside and preach, and in 1250 delivered at the papal court a sermon denouncing the curia's practice of granting English benefices to absentee Italians as the cause of the people's ruin. He refused a papal provision in 1253 in writing. The dictionary records Grosseteste as the model of what a bishop should be and had almost never been: resident, learned, pastoral and willing to tell Rome to its face that it was destroying souls for revenue.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a benefice as an ecclesiastical living; residence as the act of dwelling in a place; visitation as the inspection of a church by a superior; provision as the appointment to a benefice; and remonstrance as a strong representation of reasons against a measure.

expand to see more

BENEFICE, n. Literally, a benefit, advantage or kindness; in church affairs, an ecclesiastical living; a church endowed with a revenue.

RESIDENCE, n. The act of abiding or dwelling in a place for some continuance of time; the place of abode.

VISITATION, n. A judicial visit or examination of a corporation or church, by a superior, to inquire into its manner of conducting affairs.

PROVISION, n. In church affairs, the appointment of a successor to a benefice not yet vacant, by the pope.

REMONSTRANCE, n. Show; discovery; a strong representation of reasons against a measure, either in person or in writing.

Key Scripture

Eze 33:7 — "So thou, O son of man, I have set thee a watchman unto the house of Israel; therefore thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me."

Mal 2:7 — "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts."

Act 20:27 — "For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God."

1Pe 5:2 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind;"

Modern Corruption

Largest medieval English diocese, see of Robert Grosseteste, who denounced to the papal court the granting of English benefices to absentee Italians.

expand to see more

The corruption to name is the benefice held for its income by a man who never sees the parish, which Grosseteste attacked at the source and which outlived him by three centuries. A cure of souls given as a salary to an absentee is not a minor administrative fault; it leaves a village without preaching for a generation. Ezekiel states the office that such an arrangement abolishes, and it is a duty of speech: “thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7).

The second paragraph names the principle to recover. The priest's mouth is the people's access to instruction, “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth” (Mal 2:7); Paul's claim on his own ministry is completeness, “For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27); and Peter forbids both compulsion and greed in the motive while commanding the work itself, to feed the flock “not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind” (1Pe 5:2). Grosseteste visited every parish in the biggest diocese in England. The dictionary notes that this was thought eccentric.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew tsaphah (H6822), a watchman; Hebrew da'ath (H1847), knowledge; Greek boule (G1012), counsel.

expand to see more

Hebrew tsaphah (H6822) — to look out, to keep watch; “thou shalt hear the word at my mouth”, Ezekiel 33:7.

Hebrew zahar (H2094) — to warn, to admonish; “and warn them from me”, Ezekiel 33:7.

Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge, perception; “For the priest's lips should keep knowledge”, Malachi 2:7.

Greek boule (G1012) — counsel, purpose, determination; “all the counsel of God”, Acts 20:27.

Greek aischrokerdos (G0147) — for base gain, greedily; “not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind”, 1 Peter 5:2.

Usage

"“thou shalt hear the word at my mouth, and warn them from me” (Eze 33:7) — the office an absentee abolishes."

"“For the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — the people's access to instruction."

"“For I have not shunned to declare unto you all the counsel of God” (Act 20:27) — the standard of completeness."
